assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 20,000 ops/s at peak. An 'op' is one editor event, not one page view: ~80% are collaborative edit/keystroke messages on an open WebSocket, 4% presence heartbeats, and only 16% are HTTP requests (open, save, run).

assumptions.subject: collab
assumptions.statement: Collaboration servers are sticky per document: every editor on a doc lands on the same instance, so instances scale by DOCUMENT count, not by op rate. 2,200 ops/s per instance covers CRDT merge + fan-out to the other editors on that doc.

assumptions.subject: runner
assumptions.statement: Code execution dominates the bill: ~25 runs/s per instance (3 concurrent sandboxes at ~120 ms per short run). Long-running or GPU workloads are NOT modelled and would change this tier by an order of magnitude.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Redis is run as a 2-node cluster over a split keyspace, so the engine's additive capacity is right. A primary+replica pair would NOT double write capacity.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Single PostgreSQL primary at ~8,000 rps. It is a single point of failure as drawn; a standby is an availability decision, not a capacity one, so it is not in the capacity model.

assumptions.subject: runner-headroom
assumptions.statement: The sandbox pool is deliberately held near 55% utilisation, not at the 85% ceiling. Queueing multiplies a user-visible wait: the same 120 ms run would feel like ~800 ms at 85%. Headroom is the feature on a Run button, and it is why the runner tier is the largest line on the bill.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: The monthly figure is COMPUTE only. The CDN, load balancer and object store have no honest per-instance price, and no egress/storage volumes are declared, so their bill is not in the total — a real workspace platform pays real money for blob storage and egress.

_library.summary: Browser code editor with live collaboration and sandboxed code execution.
